title: Google and Constellation Find 890 MW of New Power Inside Running Reactors
source_used: Global Data Center Hub (newsletter analysis of the Constellation and Google announcements)
key_facts: Google and Constellation Energy announced the agreement on 6 Oct 2026: 3,590 MW in two contracts.

A 20-year power purchase agreement backs 890 MW of added output at 11 reactors in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey; Constellation says it will invest more than $4.3 billion; first uprate by 2028, all 890 MW before the end of 2032.
A separate 15-year supply agreement covers 2,700 MW from Constellation's existing PJM fleet, keeping those plants on the grid; only the 890 MW (about 25 percent) is new capacity.
An uprate raises the maximum licensed power of an operating reactor; the Nuclear Regulatory Commission must approve every increase.
PJM's independent market monitor says its 2028/2029 capacity auction cleared 6,831.3 MW short of the reliability target and names data centre load growth as the primary reason.
Commercial terms are private; Google says the deal comes at no cost to other ratepayers; the unit list and split of the 890 MW are not yet disclosed.

The agreement also includes demand response (Google can cut non-critical use in grid emergencies) and a five-year technology alliance bringing Google Cloud and Gemini Enterprise into Constellation's operations.
quote_evidence: The deal adds 890 MW of new nuclear capacity to PJM by upgrading existing reactors.
When you count new capacity, use 890 MW.
why_it_matters_hint: Only 890 of the 3,590 megawatts is new power, and the grid it joins is short of its reliability target mainly because of data centre demand.
notes: Event is 6 Oct 2026 and our 7 Oct edition carried it (Quartz, relaying the companies); WSJ and Yahoo Finance also covered it on 6 Oct. Today's piece is a newsletter analysis, so the news is older and the new part is context. The newsletter rests on Constellation's announcement and Google's post (and other outlets such as POWER and the American Nuclear Society); no original-reporter outlet beyond those is named.
